title.en: History: Social Transformation in Tamil Nadu

text.en: Meena saw a poster of a leader fighting for equal rights. "Periyar," said her teacher.

Tamil Nadu saw great social change in the twentieth century. The Justice Party, formed in 1916, worked for greater representation for non-Brahmins in jobs and education. Periyar E. V. Ramasamy led the Self-Respect Movement from 1925 against caste and superstition.
Women's rights were pushed by Muthulakshmi Reddy, who worked to end the devadasi system, and by the Self-Respect Movement. Reforms included temple entry, free education and the mid-day meal scheme.
Leaders such as Dr Ambedkar's thoughts, Iyothee Thass and later Kamaraj, Annadurai and Karunanidhi shaped Tamil Nadu's welfare policies, including reservation and scholarships.

Modern Tamil Nadu's remarkable progress in education, healthcare and social equality did not happen by accident—it grew from a century of bold reform movements.

board.text: Why Tamil Nadu leads in social justice & schools

text.en: The transformation began with the Tamil Renaissance: nineteenth-century European-born scholar Robert Caldwell proved Tamil's ancient Dravidian independence, while C. W. Thamotharampillai and U. V. Swaminatha Iyer rescued Sangam palm-leaf classics.

board.text: Tamil Renaissance: U. V. Swaminatha Iyer & Sangam

text.en: Poet Sundaranar's Manonmaniam honoured 'Tamil Thai', Parithimar Kalaignar fought to grant Tamil classical language status, and Maraimalai Adigal championed the Pure Tamil (Tani Tamil Iyakkam) movement.
Meanwhile, Pandit Iyothee Thass (1845–1914) started Dravida Pandian and Oru Paisa Tamilan, campaigning for free education, reservation and equal dignity for oppressed communities.

board.text: Pandit Iyothee Thass: pioneer of social justice

text.en: In the 1910s, non-Brahmin leaders noticed deep imbalance in Madras government jobs and colleges, forming Dr. C. Natesanar's Madras Dravidian Association and opening hostels for non-Brahmin students.
In 1916, Sir Pitti Theagarayar, Dr T. M. Nair and C. Natesanar founded the South Indian Liberal Federation—popularly the Justice Party—and won elections in 1920.

Between 1920 and 1937, Justice Party governments passed India's first Communal Reservation G.O.s, set up the Staff Selection Board, granted women voting rights (1921), and pioneered free school breakfasts in Madras Corporation schools.

board.text: 1921: Women vote & first Madras school meals!

text.en: Alongside legislative power, Periyar E. V. Ramasamy left the Congress in 1925 and launched the Self-Respect Movement (Suyamariyathai Iyakkam) to strike at caste and superstition.
Periyar championed rationalism, women's property and divorce rights, simple inter-caste Self-Respect marriages without priests, and Tamil script reform via Kudiyarasu and Viduthalai.
Even earlier in 1924, Periyar crossed into Kerala to lead the Vaikom Satyagraha for temple-road access—earning the title 'Vaikom Veerar' (Hero of Vaikom).
In 1929, the Chengalpattu Self-Respect Conference passed historic resolutions demanding equal ancestral property rights for women—sixty years before national law caught up!
Women themselves led the charge! Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy—India's first woman legislator and Chennai's Adyar Cancer Institute founder—sponsored the law ending the exploitative Devadasi system in 1930.

board.text: Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy abolishes Devadasi system

text.en: Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar, S. Dharmambal (who campaigned for Tamil teachers' pay), and Neelambikai Ammaiyar stood beside Periyar, who was honoured as 'Periyar' by the 1938 Tamil Nadu Women's Conference!
Earlier too, Rettaimalai Srinivasan and M. C. Rajah represented Dalit voices in legislatures and Round Table Talks alongside Dr B. R. Ambedkar.
Meanwhile, workers organised India's first modern trade union—Madras Labour Union (1918)—with M. Singaravelar pioneering May Day celebrations in 1923.

board.text: 1918 Madras Labour Union & Singaravelar May Day

text.en: In 1944 at Salem, Periyar merged the Justice Party into Dravidar Kazhagam (DK) as a non-electoral social reform movement.
Post-independence, Chief Minister K. Kamaraj turned schools into community beacons via free education and expanded mid-day meals so poverty never kept children out of class.
C. N. Annadurai, M. Karunanidhi and M. G. Ramachandran expanded Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation policy, nutritious noon-meal scheme and primary health centres into every village.
Check the inspiring results today: higher women's college enrolment, stronger healthcare, lower poverty and respected classical Tamil scholarship.
Notice also how Dr Muthulakshmi Reddy married legislation with welfare—both passing laws against unfair customs and building schools and hospitals.
Trace the century-long thread: Tamil Renaissance -> 1916 Justice Party -> 1925 Self-Respect -> women's laws -> free school & health welfare.
Learning Tamil Nadu's social transformation teaches that democracy shines brightest when dignity, rational thought and equal opportunity reach every family.

problem.en: How did Tamil Nadu's early twentieth-century reform movements empower women decades ahead of their time?
